But wait... there's more!

In January, SoftBank's SB Energy, the developer building the massive Ohio and Texas data center campuses, granted warrants to OpenAI as a "lease incentive" for signing a data center lease in Milam County, Texas. That's right: the landlord paid the tenant, in equity, to rent the building. Some of those warrants were forfeited in August when OpenAI signed the 20-year Ohio lease, but ¥542 billion ($3.4 billion) of them still sit on SoftBank's balance sheet as a derivative liability.

And here is the punchline: because the warrants get more valuable as SB Energy does, every time the data center business is marked higher, SoftBank books a loss, ¥204 billion in the first half, plus another ¥136 billion of share-based compensation for the unit's staff for the same reason. A business whose success shows up as a loss is a neat trick even by AI-bubble standards.

But the circularity doesn't end there:

Nvidia, the exclusive chip supplier for the Ohio campus, has wired $1.5 billion to SB Energy under a share issuance agreement and is providing credit support for OpenAI on the first 4.25 gigawatts. So the chip vendor (NVDA) funds the landlord (Softbank) and backstops the tenant (OpenAI), who then buys the chips (NVDA).

SoftBank Corp, the listed Japanese telecom arm, sold its SB Energy stake to Vision Fund 2 and booked an ¥80 billion gain. One SoftBank pocket selling to another (for a "profit"): the gain vanishes on consolidation, but it looks great at the telco, and a whole bunch of clueless Japanese momentum-chasers buy something that moves higher.

The Vision Funds, meanwhile, marked down their stakes in SoftBank's own subsidiaries, mainly SB7 (the turbine buyer) and PayPay, by ¥364 billion. That one vanishes on consolidation too.

And SB Energy's IPO, which was supposed to crystallize a $50 billion-plus valuation, has been frozen since September due to regulatory issues well before the midterms.

Gather round folks, because just when you thought Masa Son would not catalyze the bursting of the next bubble... well, read for yourselves

SoftBank bought 87 million Intel shares for $2 billion last year. By the end of March the stake was worth $3.8 billion, and by the end of September $10.5 billion, good for a ¥1.06 trillion gain in the first half. 

Instead of selling, in August SoftBank did something much more, well, SoftBank: it raised $7.35 billion through prepaid forward contracts on its entire Intel stake, structured as collars with a floor and a cap. In English, it borrowed more than three times what it paid for the stock, pledged every share, and sold away the upside above the cap to pay for the downside protection.

What happened next? Intel shares kept climbing after the ink dried, which means the capped contracts moved against SoftBank, to the tune of a ¥322 billion ($2 billion) derivative loss in less than two months. And because Intel still finished the September quarter below where it started, SoftBank also booked a ¥270 billion valuation loss on the shares themselves.

So in a single quarter Masa managed to lose money on the stock and on the hedge. That takes sheer talent.

The fine print is even better: of the ¥1.65 trillion of Intel shares pledged, the banks have "rights of use" over ¥1.1 trillion, meaning they are free to lend out or otherwise use SoftBank's collateral.

Instead of selling, in August SoftBank did something much more, well, SoftBank: it raised $7.35 billion through prepaid forward contracts on its entire Intel stake, structured as collars with a floor and a cap. In English, it borrowed more than three times what it paid for the stock, pledged every share, and sold away the upside above the cap to pay for the downside protection.

What happened next? Intel shares kept climbing after the ink dried, which means the capped contracts moved against SoftBank, to the tune of a ¥322 billion ($2 billion) derivative loss in less than two months. And because Intel still finished the September quarter below where it started, SoftBank also booked a ¥270 billion valuation loss on the shares themselves.

So in a single quarter Masa managed to lose money on the stock and on the hedge. That takes sheer talent.

The fine print is even better: of the ¥1.65 trillion of Intel shares pledged, the banks have "rights of use" over ¥1.1 trillion, meaning they are free to lend out or otherwise use SoftBank's collateral.

🔥No official U.S. CPI YoY number today — but we can still estimate it.

Because of the 2025 government shutdown, BLS never collected October 2025 CPI data, leaving it unable to calculate the usual year-over-year comparison for today’s release.

We backfilled the missing October 2025 observations with Bloomberg-derived estimates. On that basis, headline CPI is running at roughly 4.02% YoY in October, up from 3.74% in September.

The contribution breakdown is also notable:

• Core services: +2.06 percentage points
• Energy: +1.33 pp
• Food: +0.41 pp
• Core goods: +0.19 pp
That comes alongside the official October monthly readings of +0.4% headline and +0.3% core, both above consensus.

Methodology: Missing September 2025 weights are estimated by updating December 2024 weights for subsequent price changes, with the same weights used for October. Missing October 2025 index values are estimated as the geometric mean of September and November 2025.

These are Bloomberg-derived estimates, not official BLS figures.
